text: Every script in this chapter has called an external system — a webhook, a ticketing API, Teams, Slack — and every one of those calls can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with your code. A script that only handles the happy path isn't incomplete, it's dangerous: a swallowed exception mid-playbook can leave a ticket half updated or a block half applied, with nobody aware it happened. This lesson's goal is making failure a handled, expected branch instead of a crash.

Start by sorting failures into two buckets. A timeout or a 503 is usually transient — the same request will probably work if you try again shortly. A 401 or a malformed request is permanent — retrying the identical request fails the identical way every time, and only wastes time or trips a rate limit. Once you know a failure is retryable, back off instead of retrying instantly, waiting progressively longer with a little randomness so many failed callers don't retry in lockstep. And wrap any action with a real side effect in one reusable idempotency key.

call_with_backoff wraps any function call in that retry logic. Each failed, retryable attempt waits roughly double the previous delay, capped and padded with a little jitter, so attempt three waits around eight or nine seconds rather than a fixed interval. A non-retryable exception, or the final attempt, re-raises immediately instead of burning through the rest of the retry budget on a request that was never going to succeed in the first place.

Backoff answers when to retry; an idempotency key answers what happens if the first attempt actually worked and only the response got lost. Generate the key once, before the retry loop starts, and send that same key with every attempt of that one logical action — a well-built API recognizes the repeated key and returns the original result instead of blocking the same IP, or creating the same ticket, a second time. Minting a fresh key per attempt defeats the whole mechanism.

Finish with structured, JSON-formatted error logs, including the alert's event_id on every line, so a human can trace one alert's full journey across every step it touched when a playbook fails partway through. That closes the chapter: webhook receipt, ticket creation, ChatOps notification, and remediation now all share one defensive pattern — classify the error, back off, retry safely with one idempotency key, and log it so someone can actually act on it.
